content: An orphan patient is a term used in healthcare to describe a patient who has become lost within the medical system or does not have a primary healthcare provider managing their care. Typically, a primary healthcare provider, such as a general practitioner or family doctor, is responsible for addressing basic health needs and coordinating referrals to specialists for more complex medical issues. Patients without such a provider are often referred to as no-family-doctor patients. Healthcare professionals and insiders generally agree that orphan patients tend to receive suboptimal care compared to those who have a designated gatekeeper overseeing and coordinating their medical treatment. Several factors contribute to the orphan patient issue in North America. These include challenges in maintaining an adequate supply of qualified healthcare providers and ensuring their availability in the right locations and at the right times. Additionally, the problem is exacerbated by a growing patient population, an aging demographic, and an increasing prevalence of chronic illnesses such as diabetes and obesity. Furthermore, patients today have higher expectations for medical care, and the number of defined medical conditions requiring treatment has expanded. The complexity of managing diseases has also increased; for example, the standard treatment for heart attacks is now significantly more labor-intensive than it was a decade ago. Although the term orphan patient has gained more attention in recent years, it has been in use for decades, with references as early as 1988 in the New England Journal of Medicine. Addressing the orphan patient problem is inherently complex due to its multifactorial nature. While it is not feasible to reduce the population or rapidly increase the number of healthcare providers due to the lengthy training process, several strategies have been proposed to mitigate the issue. These include expanding the roles of alternative healthcare providers, such as nurse practitioners and hospitalists, and utilizing Telehealth services to provide public medical information. Technological advancements, such as electronic medical records and telemedicine, can also enhance the efficiency of existing healthcare providers. Additionally, public health initiatives, such as smoking cessation programs and fitness campaigns, aim to reduce the overall burden of illness within communities. Political interventions, such as community-wide smoking bans and mandatory seatbelt regulations, can also play a role in improving public health outcomes, often with or without direct involvement from medical professionals.
